heading: No SAE dictionary size gives a complete, atomic set of features
definition: larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents, and larger SAEs also add novel latents, so no dictionary size gives a complete, atomic set of features.
summary: Independent studies on GPT-2 Small, Llama-3.1-8B, text embeddings and a model one study does not name also find that larger SAEs add latents unlike any in smaller SAEs, but the evidence is weak. The claim that larger-SAE latents break down into smaller-SAE latents, so that no size gives an atomic set, rests only on the original group's meta-SAE work (an SAE trained on another SAE's decoder directions).

suggested_status.by_scale: By clause: 'larger SAEs add novel latents' is R2. 'Larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents' and the conclusion 'no dictionary size gives a complete, atomic set' are R1. Theory: arXiv:2606.02385 only; it supports V5 in the wide limit and limits it at finite λ. <1B (GPT-2 Small; the script buckets it as size 'not stated'): the novel-latent part is R2, reproduced with weak measures by lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak (matching ratios), which the studies index does not flag as sharing authors with an original. lw:baJyjpktzmcmRfosq repeats the original's experiment and shares an author with it, so it adds only R1 evidence. The decomposition/atomicity part is R1, because only the original and the meta-SAE post test it, and the two share one setup and an author (Bart Bussmann). 1-10B: novel-latent part: Gemma 2 2B in the original, plus one asserted, unmeasured novel-latent example on Llama-3.1-8B from another group (arXiv:2410.20526; its author list shares no author with an original), so a weak R2 at most; decomposition part: untested at this size (no study). 10-100B and >100B: no studies (counts: versions.V5.studies_by_size has only 'not stated' and '1-10B'). Model not stated: arXiv:2512.02194 (no SAME GROUP flag), novel latents at 65536 -> 4096.
suggested_status.reason:
Correlational/probing: decoder-cosine matching and meta-SAE decompositions. Causal intervention: adding or swapping latents into an SAE and measuring reconstruction MSE; this intervenes on the dictionary, not the model. Theory: arXiv:2606.02385.

Author overlap (the studies index flags overlap with any original; V5's linked original is arXiv:2502.04878, counts: versions.V5.original_sources_linked):
- The studies index flags SAME GROUP on lw:baJyjpktzmcmRfosq and lw:TMAmHh4DdMr4nCSr5. This matches counts versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 2. Both posts are by Bart Bussmann, an author of arXiv:2502.04878, so they count as the original group's extension (R1), never as independent.
- The index flags none of lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak, arXiv:2512.02194, arXiv:2410.20526, arXiv:2408.00657 or arXiv:2606.02385. The author list of arXiv:2410.20526 shares no author with an original.

Novel latents in larger SAEs (R2), by setting:
- GPT-2 Small: lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak (22.27-47.15% matched).
- Model not stated: arXiv:2512.02194 (33.8-73.8% novel across objectives; peer-reviewed).
- Llama-3.1-8B: arXiv:2410.20526, one asserted example.
- Text embeddings: arXiv:2408.00657, qualitative.
None of these is flagged as sharing authors with an original. The evidence is weak: lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak does not tell split children from novel latents, and arXiv:2512.02194 does not state its model.

Decomposition into smaller-SAE latents (R1) rests on the original's meta-SAE (arXiv:2502.04878#R10, 55.47% variance explained) and the meta-SAE post. The post uses the same setup, shares an author with the original, and is qualitative and lossy. lw:baJyjpktzmcmRfosq repeats the original's own numbers. The 'no dictionary size gives a complete, atomic set' conclusion is tested only across specific size pairs, and its atomicity half rests on the decomposition evidence.

Conflicts: the one V5 conflict (lw:baJyjpktzmcmRfosq#r7 and lw:baJyjpktzmcmRfosq#r12 vs lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak#r1-r6) differs in magnitude only, and both verdicts are supports. The conflict index's two GPT-2 Small groups (measurement; scaling) pair the original's rows with other studies' rows on different measures (states observed vs partial), not opposite results. Neither changes a level.

Relevant counts:
- versions.V5.verdicts.challenges.studies = 0
- versions.V5.studies_with_limits_scope = 3
- versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 2
- versions.V5.tested_with_uncertainty = 0

The whole version therefore stands at R1. Its decomposition clause and the 'atomic' conclusion rest on the original group alone. The novel-latent clause on its own is R2.
suggested_status.open_questions:
Results that would change the level:
- An independent group (no author shared with an original) decomposes larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, with numbers, ideally on a non-GPT-2 family (would raise the decomposition part to R2).
- Activation or input-coverage tests that separate novel latents from split children (would firm up the novel-latent part).
- A width sweep showing whether the novel-latent share ever falls to the same-seed level (the original's 94% reconstruction latents at cosine > 0.7), as arXiv:2606.02385's finite-λ result allows (could challenge 'no dictionary size').
- Any model above 10B, or a chat-tuned model.
- Uncertainty estimates.
- An author_match.py check of lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak and arXiv:2512.02194 against the authors of the originals (Towards Monosemanticity, arXiv:2409.14507, arXiv:2502.04878). Their author lists are not in the author file used for this revision, so their independence rests only on the studies index having no flag for them. If either shares an author, the novel-latent R2 would rest on the remaining unflagged studies.

source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
source.authors: Patrick Leask; Bart Bussmann; Michael Pearce; J. Bloom; Curt Tigges; N. A. Moubayed; Lee Sharkey; Neel Nanda

original_result.setup: They stitched latents from one SAE into another, across GPT-2 Small SAEs of 768 to 12288 latents and Gemma Scope SAEs of 16384 and 32768 latents, and trained a meta-SAE on a 49152-latent GPT-2 SAE's decoder directions.
original_result.result: Larger-SAE latents unlike any smaller-SAE latent (highest decoder cosine below 0.7 on GPT-2 Small, 0.4 on Gemma 2 2B) tended to lower reconstruction error when added to the smaller SAE. A 2304-latent meta-SAE, with on average 4 meta-latents active per latent, explained 55.47% of the variance in the 49152-latent SAE's decoder directions.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Llama Scope described its 32x-wide SAE's Brexit feature as new, not built from 8x-wide SAE features.
For all three SAE types, a 65536-latent SAE had novel latents, absent from a 4096-latent one.
On astrophysics (astro-ph) paper embeddings, a larger SAE had features unrelated to any in smaller SAEs.
For data along many distinct directions (rays), theory predicts splitting continues indefinitely as dictionary width grows.
Some latents of a 49152-latent GPT-2 Small SAE decomposed interpretably into meta-SAE and 3072-latent SAE latents.
A 1536-latent GPT-2 SAE's novel latents held information a 768-latent SAE lacked and cut its MSE.
In GPT-2 Small, only 22–47% of larger-SAE latents closely matched a smaller-SAE latent's decoder direction.
Ordered O-SAE training cut the larger SAE's novel-latent share from 73.8% (BatchTopK) to 33.8%, not zero.
With a finite sparsity penalty λ and ray-clustered data, theory implies splitting stops at some width.
Meta-SAE decompositions of SAE-49152 latents were lossy, leaving a possibly unique residual.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: Decomposition of larger-SAE latents into combinations of smaller-SAE latents outside GPT-2 Small. The only decomposition rows (meta-SAE and swap-in tests) are on GPT-2 Small layer 8, and they come from the original and the meta-SAE post, which share one setup.

untested.what: An empirical test of whether any dictionary size is complete or atomic. Studies show novel latents only across specific size pairs; only the theory study (arXiv:2606.02385) addresses a finite width that is complete in loss terms.

wording_issues.phrase: larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents
wording_issues.issue: Decompositions are partial and mostly qualitative. The original's meta-SAE (2304 latents, about 4 active per source latent) explains 55.47% of the variance in decoder directions of a 49152-latent GPT-2 SAE (R10, partial). Its meta-latents have 'high' max cosine to SAE-3072 latents, with no number given (R12). In the meta-SAE post, meta-latents and the top-cosine SAE-3072 latents give similar, interpretable decompositions (r5-r7, qualitative case studies). The post also replaces the meta-SAE's decoder with the max-cosine latents from four SAEs (768 to 6144 latents) and fine-tunes the encoder. This reconstructs only slightly worse than the meta-SAE, and no number is given (not in rows). The post calls the meta-SAE decompositions lossy, and says the residual may be unique (r5, limits_scope).

wording_issues.phrase: larger SAEs also add novel latents
wording_issues.issue: 'Novel' is set by a max-decoder-cosine cut-off (0.7 for GPT-2 and 0.4 for Gemma Scope in the original; the stitching post calls 0.7 somewhat arbitrary). In the dataset-influence post, unmatched latents may be split children rather than novel ones. The Llama-3.1-8B case is one asserted example. The novel share depends on the objective: 73.8% for BatchTopK vs 33.8% for O-SAE.

wording_issues.phrase: so no dictionary size gives a complete, atomic set of features
wording_issues.issue: The empirical tests compare specific size pairs: 65536 -> 4096 only (arXiv:2512.02194); up to 12,288 latents on GPT2-small (lw:ATsvzF77ZsfWzyTak). None tests every size. In theory, for finite λ with ray-clustered data, a finite width is complete in loss terms: extra width beyond the narrowest global optimum gives no loss gain (arXiv:2606.02385 r4, limits_scope). Wider solutions, such as one atom per datapoint, are equally optimal, and the authors say splitting continues 'ad infinitum' in the wide limit, so this does not mean splitting ends.

The two properties rest on different evidence. Completeness rests on novel-latent results (stitching, matching ratios, single examples). Atomicity rests on decomposition results, and only the original and the meta-SAE post (same GPT-2 Small layer 8, SAE-49152 setup) test that. The non-original studies other than the meta-SAE post each list decomposition as untested, and the meta-SAE post lists novel latents as untested.

method_sensitivity.factor: Cosine threshold and matching rule for 'novel' vs 'similar' latents
method_sensitivity.what: The original uses 0.7 for GPT-2 SAEs and 0.4 for Gemma Scope SAEs (R5, R6; method-sensitivity line), and says these were set from exploratory analysis. It also sweeps the threshold. An ROC curve classifies latents as novel or reconstruction at varying max-cosine thresholds, scored against whether adding the latent lowers MSE (Appendix Figure 13; figure only, no AUC stated). Figure 4 plots each GPT2-1536 latent's MSE change against its max cosine to GPT2-768 (R5). Its same-size, different-seed control classifies 94% of latents as reconstruction latents at cosine > 0.7 (not in rows). The stitching post calls 0.7 somewhat arbitrary, and its V5 rows use 0.7 (r7, r9). The dataset-influence post's rows also use 0.7 (r1-r6), and it notes a limitation from not using Hungarian matching. The meta-SAE post says relationships differ between meta-SAE and smaller-SAE comparisons.
Novel-feature percentage in 65536 -> 4096 stitching: BatchTopK 73.8%, Random MSAE 52.7%, O-SAE 33.8%. Reconstruction percentage: 21.2%, 11.4% and 64.8%.

method_sensitivity.factor: Size ratio between the two SAEs compared
method_sensitivity.what: GPT2-small layer 8 Top-k SAEs, OpenWebText. Matched share: 25.56% for 12,288 in 3,072 (r1); 39.36% for 12,288 in 6,144 (r3); 47.15% for 6,144 in 3,072 (r5).

Same comparisons, OpenWebText vs TinyStories: 25.56% vs 22.27% (12,288 in 3,072), 39.36% vs 40.62% (12,288 in 6,144), 47.15% vs 43.47% (6,144 in 3,072). The authors report that dataset affects matching ratios.

method_sensitivity.factor: Sparsity penalty λ and data structure (theory)
method_sensitivity.what: In the wide limit, splitting continues toward one atom per datapoint. With finite λ and ray-clustered data, a narrowest global optimum exists, and extra width beyond it gives no loss gain (r4). Wider solutions, such as one atom per datapoint, are equally optimal, so this does not mean splitting stops. The study also reports that optimality-condition violations grow with distance from the training layer or dataset.

method_sensitivity.factor: SAE k and dictionary size n (text-embedding SAEs)
method_sensitivity.what: Max nearest-neighbour decoder cosine between features of different SAEs falls as n grows at fixed k (r1, Fig. 9a) and as k grows at fixed n (r2, Fig. 9b). Both rows pool astro-ph and cs.LG, are figure only, and are cannot_determine rows from the V1 pack. Features recur across sizes more at lower k (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 18a). At k=16, r6 counts over 1100 recurrent triplets (min cosine > 0.95; n = 3072, 6144, 9216); that row is cannot_determine, and its verdict fix says the appendix contradicts itself. Family in-block vs off-block activation-similarity ratios (Ddiag/Doff) are given as numbers in Table 1, ranging 0.89-5.87 by dataset and (k, n) (not in rows). The Appendix E.2 activation-similarity ratios are in Fig. 19.

status_amendment.public_note: The status now counts two follow-up posts by an author of the original paper as that group's own work, not as independent checks: other groups have reproduced, with weak measures, that larger SAEs add new latents, but the claim that larger-SAE latents break down into smaller-SAE ones, and so the 'atomic' part of the conclusion, still rests on the original group alone. The overall level is unchanged.
